DNA: The molecule that carries genetic information: a very long thread made of four letters, A, C, G and T, repeated in a precise order.
genome: All the DNA of an organism: in humans, about 3.1 billion letters, in two copies in each cell.
nucleus: The central compartment of a cell, closed by a membrane, where DNA is stored.
GM12878: A line of human cells (white blood cells from a female donor) grown in the laboratory, among the most studied in the world; this model is built for it.
simulated: Computed by a program that follows known rules, rather than observed directly in the cell.
predicted: Inferred by the model from other data, without having been measured directly.
planted: Placed by hand in a simulation, at a chosen spot, to test a rule; not read from a measurement.
illustrative: Shown to give a fair idea of the shape, without claiming the exact position.
chromosome: One of the 46 pieces of a human cell's DNA thread. We inherit 23 from our mother and 23 from our father.
chromosome territory: The region of the nucleus that a chromosome occupies: each one stays in its own, without mixing with the others.
compartment: One of the two kinds of neighbourhood in the genome: A, active and open; B, silent and tight. Regions of the same kind gather together in the nucleus.
gene: A passage of DNA that serves as a recipe for making a protein (or an RNA).
TAD: “Topologically associating domain”: a stretch of the DNA thread folded onto itself, whose parts mostly touch one another, bounded by CTCF proteins.
contact: Two pieces of DNA, far apart along the thread, that end up side by side in space. They are counted by a technique called Hi-C.
cohesin: A ring of proteins that encircles the DNA thread and slides it through itself, making a loop grow.
loop extrusion: The mechanism by which cohesin enlarges a loop of DNA, until it runs into CTCF boundaries.
CTCF: A protein that binds a short DNA motif, oriented one way; two CTCF facing each other stop cohesin and form the boundaries of a loop or a TAD.
enhancer: A switch in the DNA: a short region that turns a gene on, sometimes from very far away, by touching it through a loop.
promoter: The start of a gene, where its reading begins.
nucleosome: A small spool of proteins (histones) around which about 147 letters of DNA are wound.
chromatin: DNA together with the proteins that package it, including nucleosomes.
double helix: The shape of the DNA molecule: two strands wound around each other, joined by their letters.
base: A letter of DNA: A (adenine), C (cytosine), G (guanine) or T (thymine). A pairs with T, C with G.
mutation: A change in the sequence of letters of DNA.
border: The boundary between two TADs, held by CTCF proteins: the thread crosses it, but contacts hardly do.
inactive X: In women, one of the two X chromosomes, switched off and compacted to balance gene doses with men.
superdomain: A very large folded block of the inactive X, much bigger than a TAD; there are two of them.
